records.name: Āl Bū Saʿīd (Busaidi) dynasty of Oman and Zanzibar
records.scaleNote: The Busaidi state taxed and protected the main 19th-century East African slave market at Zanzibar; Sheriff and Alpers estimate tens of thousands of captives a year passed through the Zanzibar customs by the 1860s (figures vary by source and are reconstructed from British consular reports).
records.origins: An Omani dynasty that took power in Muscat c. 1749 after expelling the Persians and inherited Oman's claims to the Swahili coast, won from the Portuguese in the late 17th century. Under Sayyid Saʿīd it shifted its commercial centre to Zanzibar.
records.role_summary: The dynasty's rulers licensed caravans, farmed out customs to Indian financiers, and drew revenue from a per-head duty on enslaved people imported to Zanzibar. Enslaved Africans worked Zanzibar and Pemba's clove plantations and were re-exported to Arabia, the Gulf, Madagascar and the French islands.

roleDetail.d: Customs on captives and ivory, collected by Indian revenue farmers, were a core income of the sultanate until the 1873 closure (Sheriff).
From c. 1828 Zanzibar and Pemba became the world's largest clove producers, worked largely by enslaved mainlanders, per Britannica.
Successive treaties (1822 Moresby, 1845 Hamerton, 1873 Frere) narrowed and finally closed the seaborne trade under British naval pressure.

records.legacy: Britain declared a protectorate over Zanzibar in 1890 and slavery's legal status was abolished there in 1897 (concubines only in 1909). The Zanzibar line was overthrown in the 1964 revolution, whose violence was partly framed around the racial and class legacies of slavery; the Omani branch still rules Oman.

legacyDetail.d: The Al Said who rule Oman today descend from the same dynasty; the Zanzibar sultanate ended in January 1964.
In Tanzania, the Arab/Omani role in slavery remains a sensitive political theme, tied to memories of the 1964 revolution.

lineage.name: Haitham bin Tariq

records.today: The Al Bu Said dynasty still rules Oman: Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, cousin of the late Sultan Qaboos, succeeded in 2020. The Zanzibar line ended with the 1964 revolution, and its last sultan, Jamshid bin Abdullah, died on 30 December 2024. Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Sayyid Saʿīd ibn Sulṭān
records.scaleNote: Britannica credits him with making Zanzibar 'the commercial capital of the western Indian Ocean'; the slave-worked clove economy and caravan trade he fostered expanded East African slave exports sharply in 1830–56 (Sheriff, Alpers; volumes estimated).
records.origins: Born in Oman in 1791, he seized sole power in Muscat in 1806. Seeing the wealth of the East African coast, he campaigned against Mombasa's Mazrui rulers and made Zanzibar his main residence from the 1830s.
records.role_summary: He promoted clove planting on Zanzibar and Pemba from c. 1828, worked by enslaved Africans, and encouraged Indian financiers and Omani-Swahili caravans into the mainland interior for ivory and captives. He signed the Moresby (1822) and Hamerton (1845) treaties limiting, but not ending, the trade.

roleDetail.d: Britannica: from 1828 he developed Zanzibar and Pemba into the world's largest clove producers; the plantations depended on enslaved mainland Africans.
He farmed customs to Kutchi merchants such as Jairam Shivji, whose credit financed inland caravans (Wint; Sheriff).
Under British pressure he banned sales to Christians (1822) and export beyond his African dominions (1845), keeping the internal trade legal.

records.legacy: On his death in 1856 his realm split between sons Majid (Zanzibar) and Thuwayni (Oman), confirmed by the 1861 Canning Award. Zanzibar's Stone Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, largely reflects the wealth of his era.

legacyDetail.d: The 1861 Canning Award made the African dominions a separate sultanate.
UNESCO lists Zanzibar's Stone Town, whose 19th-century fabric grew from the clove, ivory and slave trades.

sources.label: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History — The 19th Century Slave Trade in Eastern Africa

lineage.name: Sultan bin Ahmad
lineage.note: Died on an expedition to Basra, leaving young sons under a regent.

lineage.name: Aisha bint Sultan
lineage.note: Took the regency for her younger brother and commanded troops.

lineage.name: Shivji Topan and Jairam Shivji
lineage.note: Kutchi merchants who farmed his customs and lent him money.

lineage.name: Thuwaini bin Said
lineage.note: Inherited Oman.

lineage.name: Majid bin Said
lineage.note: Inherited Zanzibar.

lineage.name: Barghash bin Said
lineage.note: Later Sultan of Zanzibar.

lineage.name: Salme bint Said (Emily Ruete)
lineage.note: Eloped with a German merchant and wrote 'Memoirs of an Arabian Princess from Zanzibar', a key source on the enslaved household of the palace.

records.today: His descendants include the present Omani royal family through the Muscat line (Sultan Haitham bin Tariq). The Zanzibar line ended with the 1964 revolution. Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Barghash bin Saʿīd
records.scaleNote: As sultan he presided over Zanzibar's trade until signing the 1873 Frere treaty, which banned seaborne slave exports from the mainland and closed the Zanzibar slave market (Britannica; The National Archives).
records.origins: A son of Sayyid Saʿīd, he attempted a coup against his brother Majid in 1859 and was exiled to Bombay. He succeeded Majid in 1870.
records.role_summary: He initially resisted British demands, but under the threat of naval blockade signed the treaty of 5 June 1873 negotiated by Sir Bartle Frere and consul John Kirk, closing the Zanzibar market. In 1876 he issued proclamations against slave caravans on the mainland, though slavery itself stayed legal.

roleDetail.d: The Frere treaty banned the transport of enslaved people by sea from the mainland and closed public markets in his dominions.
Accounts agree Britain threatened a blockade of Zanzibar to force agreement; the treaty alienated Omani planters.
Smuggling by dhow and overland caravans to the Somali coast continued after 1873, per Kirk's own reports.

records.legacy: Barghash built the Beit al-Ajaib ('House of Wonders') and modernised Zanzibar Town, but lost mainland territory to German and British partition in 1885–86. The Anglican Christ Church Cathedral now stands on the site of the market he closed.

legacyDetail.t: Christ Church on the market site.
legacyDetail.d: The Universities' Mission to Central Africa bought the market ground in 1873 and laid the cathedral's foundation stone on Christmas Day 1873.
His loss of the coastal hinterland to German East Africa helped end Zanzibar's role as the caravan hub.

lineage.note: Founder of the Zanzibar slave-and-clove economy.

records.today: Barghash's House of Wonders (Beit al-Ajaib) still stands in Stone Town, and Christ Church Cathedral occupies the site of the slave market he closed. The Zanzibar sultanate he ruled ended in 1964. Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Tippu Tip (Ḥamad bin Muḥammad al-Murjebi)
records.scaleNote: Britannica calls him the most prominent late-19th-century Arab-Swahili trader in Central Africa, leading caravans of up to c. 4,000 men; ivory was his chief interest but his raids and caravans produced large numbers of captives (numbers undocumented).
records.origins: Born in Zanzibar to an Omani-Swahili trading family with Nyamwezi connections, he joined his father's caravans to the interior as a young man. By the late 1860s he led large armed expeditions.
records.role_summary: He built a loosely organised trading state in the Maniema region of the eastern Congo basin, extracting ivory and captives through raids, alliances and tribute; captives carried ivory to the coast and many were sold. He helped Stanley (1876–77) and in 1887 accepted appointment by King Leopold II as governor of the Stanley Falls district of the Congo Free State.

roleDetail.d: Britannica stresses ivory as his main goal; captives were seized in raids and used as porters, plantation workers and trade goods.
In 1887 he became governor of the Falls district of the Congo Free State, an arrangement that collapsed; he left in 1890.
His Swahili autobiography (Maisha ya Hamed bin Muhammed el Murjebi) is a rare first-person source from a slave and ivory trader.

records.legacy: He retired to Zanzibar, where he died in 1905, wealthy from clove plantations worked by enslaved people. Leopold's Congo Free State later used the 'Arab slave trade' as justification for its own violent conquest (1892–94), a propaganda framing historians now treat critically.

legacyDetail.d: Belgian 'anti-slavery' campaigns against the Arab-Swahili traders legitimised Leopold's own forced-labour regime.
Tippu Tip's house survives in Zanzibar's Stone Town as a landmark.

sources.label: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History — The 19th Century Slave Trade in Eastern Africa

lineage.name: Muhammad bin Juma
lineage.note: Arab-Swahili caravan trader with ties to Tabora, whose caravans Tippu Tip joined as a young man.

lineage.name: Bint Habib bin Bushir
lineage.note: Daughter of a prosperous Muscat family of the Wardi clan.

lineage.name: Tharia Topan

lineage.name: Barghash bin Said

lineage.name: David Livingstone

lineage.name: Henry Morton Stanley

lineage.name: Sefu bin Hamid

records.today: Tippu Tip's Swahili autobiography is a classic source, and a house associated with him survives in Stone Town, Zanzibar. No publicly documented descendants have been traced. His career is also cited critically for how Leopold's Congo used 'Arab slave trade' rhetoric to justify its own conquest.

records.name: Jairam Shivji (Jairam Sewji) and firm
records.scaleNote: His firm held the Zanzibar customs farm for most of 1835–1876 and, by 1850, contracts from Cape Delgado to Mogadishu; this put the duties on captives and ivory, and credit for caravans, in its hands (Wikipedia citing Sheriff; Wint).
records.origins: A Bhatia merchant from Kutch in western India, from a family that first won the Zanzibar customs contract in 1819. He became adviser and banker to Sayyid Saʿīd.
records.role_summary: As customs farmer he collected duties on goods and captives entering Zanzibar, and as banker advanced trade goods on credit to Arab and Swahili caravan leaders whose expeditions returned with ivory and enslaved people. Indian credit was thus a hidden engine of the East African trade, though most Indian financiers did not themselves deal in captives directly.

roleDetail.d: Shivji's firm regained the Zanzibar customs contract in 1835 and expanded it along the coast, including Mombasa (1837) and Mafia and Lindi (1840s).
Oxford Research Encyclopedia (Wint) describes Gujarati credit networks financing the caravan trade.
From the 1860s British consuls treated Indians in Zanzibar as British subjects and pressed them to free enslaved people they held.

records.legacy: The firm lost the customs farm in 1876 to Tharia Topan. Christ Church Zanzibar's history records that part of the old slave-market site was given by 'Mr Jairam Senji', an ironic coda.

legacyDetail.t: Gave part of the cathedral land.
legacyDetail.d: Accounts of Christ Church Cathedral record part of the 1873 market site as a gift from a Hindu merchant named Jairam Senji (Sewji's firm).
Recent scholarship stresses South Asian finance in African slaving rather than an exclusively 'Arab' trade.

sources.label: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History — Financing the Indian Ocean Slave Trade (Hollian Wint)

lineage.name: Shivji Topan
lineage.note: Muscat merchant who won the Zanzibar customs contract in 1819.

lineage.name: Madhavji Topan

lineage.name: Sayyid Saʿīd bin Sultan

lineage.name: Tharia Topan

lineage.name: Swali family
lineage.note: His family adopted the surname Swali; a street in Mundra is called Swali Sheri.

records.today: Jairam Shivji died in 1866 and the firm lost the customs farm in 1876. His family, which took the surname Swali, is remembered in a street name in Mundra, Kutch; no private living individuals are named here, and they carry no guilt for his financing of the trade.

records.name: Tharia Topan
records.scaleNote: Head of Zanzibar customs from c. 1876 (sources differ, c. 1875–80) and a leading financier of caravans and of European explorers; direct slave dealing is not documented, so his scale reflects financing rather than trafficking.
records.origins: A Khoja Ismaili from Kutch who arrived in Zanzibar poor and worked for Jairam Shivji's firm. He built his own trade in cloves, ivory and spices.
records.role_summary: He financed caravans, supplied explorers including Stanley, and from 1876 held the customs of Zanzibar under Barghash. He is often named as a financier of Tippu Tip's ventures.

roleDetail.d: Head of Zanzibar customs from c. 1876, succeeding Jairam Shivji's firm; sources differ on the exact span (c. 1875–80).
Banked caravans and European expeditions; ties to Tippu Tip are reported but less securely documented.

records.legacy: Knighted by Britain in 1890, he funded a hospital in Zanzibar and helped settle Ismaili migrants in East Africa, a community whose descendants remain prominent in the region.

legacyDetail.d: Britain knighted him in 1890 (his family recalls it as recognition of help against slavery). He began a hospital in Stone Town in the 1880s, completed after his death in Bombay in 1891; it later became the Aga Khan Polyclinic.

sources.label: The Institute of Ismaili Studies — The Voices of History: From Zanzibar to London (Farouk Topan on Sir Tharia Topan)
Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History — Financing the Indian Ocean Slave Trade (Hollian Wint)

lineage.name: Jairam Shivji's firm
lineage.note: He rose to head of its credit department.

lineage.name: Barghash bin Said
lineage.note: Gave him the customs contract and trusted him as adviser.

lineage.name: Tippu Tip
lineage.note: Received trade goods on credit from Topan for his caravans.

lineage.name: His widows
lineage.note: Continued building his charitable hospital (the Old Dispensary) after his death.

records.today: The Old Dispensary he commissioned in Stone Town in 1887 still stands. He helped settle Khoja Ismaili migrants in East Africa, a community still prominent in the region. No private living individuals are named here.

records.name: Swahili coast merchants and the sultans of Kilwa
records.scaleNote: Kilwa recovered in the 18th century largely through the slave trade, supplying French Mascarene planters from the 1770s and then Zanzibar; Alpers and Sheriff reconstruct thousands of captives a year through Kilwa by the mid-19th century.
records.origins: Muslim, African-rooted urban merchant communities of the East African coast, intermarried with Arab and Persian traders, ran Indian Ocean trade in gold and ivory from medieval times. Kilwa was among the richest Swahili towns until the Portuguese sack of 1505.
records.role_summary: Swahili traders bought captives from Yao, Makua and Nyamwezi suppliers inland and sold them to Arab, Indian, French and Portuguese buyers. In the late 18th century Kilwa became the main supplier of enslaved labour to the French Mascarenes, and in the 19th to Zanzibar's clove plantations.

roleDetail.t: Medieval trade in people was small.
roleDetail.d: Slaves were one export among gold and ivory before 1700; volume rose sharply only in the 18th–19th centuries (Swahili Coast ORE).
From the 1770s French traders bought captives at Kilwa for Île de France and Bourbon (Alpers).
Britannica notes Yao traders' networks from the Lake Malawi region to Kilwa and Mozambique Island.

records.legacy: Swahili culture and language spread inland along caravan routes partly through this trade. Kilwa Kisiwani's ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

legacyDetail.d: The Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara were inscribed by UNESCO and removed from the danger list after conservation.

sources.label: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History — Slave Trade and Urban Slavery on the Swahili Coast
UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara

lineage.name: Ali ibn al-Hassan Shirazi
lineage.note: Persian-descended prince said to have founded the Kilwa Sultanate.

lineage.name: Kilwa sultans
lineage.note: Controlled the gold trade from Sofala until the Portuguese sack of 1505.

lineage.name: Busaidi sultans
lineage.note: Omani rulers who took control of the coast and its slave trade.

records.today: Swahili language and urban culture are the lasting legacy of these merchant towns; the ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. No individual descendants are named here.

records.name: Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais
records.scaleNote: As governor of the French Mascarenes (1735–46) he built Île de France into a slave plantation and naval colony; the enslaved population of the islands grew from c. 7,200 (1735) to c. 133,000 (1807) (Richard B. Allen's estimates).
records.origins: A Breton naval officer in the service of the Compagnie des Indes. Appointed governor-general of Île de France and Bourbon in 1735.
records.role_summary: He developed Port Louis, sugar and food production, and imported enslaved labour from Madagascar, Mozambique, West Africa and India for Compagnie des Indes projects on the islands.

roleDetail.d: He governed the Mascarenes for the Compagnie des Indes 1735–46.
His public works and plantations relied on enslaved people bought from Madagascar and the East African coast.

records.legacy: He is still commemorated with a statue in Port Louis and as a founder of Mauritius; Mauritian debates over slavery memory increasingly question that commemoration.

legacyDetail.d: A statue of La Bourdonnais stands on Port Louis's waterfront.
Mauritian commemoration of slavery (1 February, Le Morne) sits alongside colonial founder memorials.

His grandson Louis-Charles became a famous chess master; no living descendants are named here.

records.name: Moulay Ismāʿīl ibn Sharīf
records.scaleNote: Britannica says his ʿAbīd al-Bukhārī grew to about 150,000 men at its peak; that figure and the force's servile status are contested (e.g. Calderón 2023). He also held European captives seized by corsairs.
records.origins: Second ruler of the ʿAlawī dynasty, proclaimed sultan in 1672 after his half-brother's death. He spent decades suppressing rivals and rebellions.
records.role_summary: From 1673 he built the ʿAbīd al-Bukhārī, a standing army of Black Moroccans—freeborn people forcibly enrolled and enslaved people bought or conscripted—whose children were bred and trained for service. He also used European captives, ransomed or enslaved, on his palace works at Meknès.

roleDetail.d: Britannica: an army of freeborn Black Moroccans and sub-Saharan slaves purchased or impressed, their sons trained in special schools.
Moroccan ulama protested his enslavement of free Black Muslims (the haratin), a famous early debate on race and slavery in Islamic law.
Corsair captives such as Thomas Pellow worked on his building projects and in his army.

records.legacy: After his death the ʿAbīd became kingmakers and brigands; they were later reorganised. His imperial city of Meknès is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

legacyDetail.d: The historic city of Meknès, built largely with forced labour, is UNESCO-listed.
Historians debate how far the ʿAbīd were enslaved soldiers versus a privileged military caste.

lineage.name: Moulay Sharif
lineage.note: Emir of Tafilalt and first sovereign of the ʿAlawī dynasty.

lineage.name: Mubarka
lineage.note: Described by the historian Ibn Zaydan as an enslaved Black woman of the Mghafra.

lineage.name: Moulay Rashid

lineage.name: Lalla Aisha Mubarka and Khnata bint Bakkar

lineage.name: Moulay Ahmad

lineage.name: Mohammed VI
lineage.note: Present king of the ʿAlawī dynasty.

records.today: The ʿAlawī dynasty still reigns in Morocco; King Mohammed VI has ruled since 1999. Moulay Ismail's imperial city of Meknès is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Sokoto Caliphate
records.scaleNote: Lovejoy calls it one of the largest slave societies in modern history; Lovejoy estimates at least 1 million and perhaps as many as 2.5 million enslaved people by c. 1900, assuming a quarter to a half of the population was enslaved (Lovejoy and Hogendorn). Its wars also produced Hausa captives sold south into the Atlantic trade.
records.origins: Founded by the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio, whose jihad (1804–08) overthrew the Hausa kings. His son Muḥammad Bello became the first sultan.
records.role_summary: Jihad and later annual campaigns against non-Muslim and 'apostate' neighbours captured large numbers of people, who were settled on plantations (ribats) or traded north across the Sahara and south to the coast. Some Muslim captives—Hausa, Nupe, Yoruba—reached Bahia, where they took part in the 1835 Malê revolt.

roleDetail.d: Lovejoy: enslaved people produced grain, cotton and indigo on plantations around Sokoto, Kano and Zaria.
The jihad's spread into Yorubaland (Ilorin, c. 1817) helped collapse Oyo, sending many Yoruba and Hausa captives to Bahia (Lovejoy; Reis).
Usman dan Fodio forbade the enslavement of free Muslims, though Lovejoy shows this was often ignored.

records.legacy: British conquest in 1903 ended the caliphate's independence; colonial authorities moved slowly, and slavery was not finally abolished in Northern Nigeria until 1936. The Sultan of Sokoto remains the spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims.

legacyDetail.d: Lovejoy and Hogendorn document the 'slow death of slavery' in Northern Nigeria, legally ending only in 1936.
The Sultan of Sokoto is still Nigeria's senior Muslim authority.

sources.label: Cambridge Core — Lovejoy, Transformations in Slavery, ch. 9: Slavery in the Savanna during the Era of the Jihads
Wikipedia — List of sultans of Sokoto

lineage.name: Abdullahi dan Fodio

lineage.name: Muhammad Bello

lineage.name: Nana Asmaʾu

Slavery in Northern Nigeria was formally ended only in 1936. Descendants of the dan Fodio family carry no guilt for the caliphate's slave raiding.

records.name: Kanem-Bornu and the al-Kanemi dynasty
records.scaleNote: Britannica's slavery article estimates the enslaved share of Bornu's population at perhaps 40% (1580–1890); Bornu was the main supplier of captives to Fezzan and Tripoli in the 19th century.
records.origins: An ancient Sahelian Muslim state around Lake Chad, ruled by the Sayfawa dynasty for centuries. After Fulani jihadists sacked its capital in 1808, the scholar-warrior Muḥammad al-Amīn al-Kānemī repelled them and became effective ruler.
records.role_summary: Bornu raided its southern neighbours and exported captives across the Sahara via Fezzan to Tripoli in exchange for horses, firearms and goods. Leo Africanus reported horses priced at up to 20 slaves each.

roleDetail.d: Britannica: captives from southern raids were used locally and sent north for horses, armour and copper.
19th-century observers (Lyon, Barth) tied the Tripoli–Fezzan trade to Bornu raids.
Al-Kanemi contested the legitimacy of the Sokoto jihad in a famous exchange of letters with Muḥammad Bello.

records.legacy: Rabih az-Zubayr conquered Bornu in 1893 and destroyed Kukawa; the al-Kanemi line was restored under colonial rule and the Shehu of Borno remains a traditional ruler in Nigeria.

legacyDetail.d: The al-Kanemi dynasty still holds the title Shehu of Borno at Maiduguri.

Wikipedia — Abubakar ibn Umar Garba el-Kanemi

lineage.note: Ancient royal house of Kanem-Bornu; mai Dunama IX rewarded al-Kanemi with power.

lineage.note: Scholar-warrior who defeated the Fulani jihadists.

Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Fezzan rulers and Murzuq caravan merchants
records.scaleNote: Murzuq was the main relay on the Bornu–Tripoli road; Britannica calls Murzuq a centre of the slave and arms trade; early-19th-century British observers reported several thousand captives a year reaching Tripoli, mostly via Fezzan (contemporary estimates vary and are not precise).
records.origins: The Awlad Muhammad dynasty made Murzuq their capital in the 16th century, diverting trade from older Zawila. Fezzan later fell under Tripoli's Qaramanli and then direct Ottoman rule.
records.role_summary: Fezzani and Ghadamesi merchants organised caravans that marched captives from Bornu and Hausaland across the desert to Tripoli, from where many were shipped to Ottoman ports. Death rates on the desert crossing were high.

roleDetail.d: Northern routes converged at Murzuq and continued south as 'the Bornu route' to Kanem, Bornu and Wadai.
Ottoman decrees against the trade (1857) were weakly enforced; Fezzan's slave trade persisted to the 1890s.

records.legacy: Bones along desert routes, recorded by 19th-century travellers, became symbols of the trade's toll. Black Libyan communities in Fezzan partly descend from enslaved people.

legacyDetail.d: Many Black Libyans in the Fezzan trace descent to enslaved people brought by the caravan trade.

lineage.name: Awlad Muhammad dynasty
lineage.note: Made Murzuq their capital and the hub of the Bornu–Tripoli caravan trade.

lineage.name: Karamanli dynasty of Tripoli
lineage.note: Autonomous Ottoman rulers who at their height controlled Fezzan.

lineage.name: Bornu
lineage.note: Main source of captives sent north through Murzuq.

records.today: No individual descendants of the Fezzan rulers or merchants are named here. Black Libyan communities in Fezzan partly descend from people enslaved in this trade.

records.name: Muḥammad ʿAlī Pasha and the Khedivate of Egypt
records.scaleNote: Egypt's 1820–21 conquest of Sudan aimed partly at enslaved soldiers; surveys cite c. 20,000 Sudanese captives a year reaching Egypt in the early period (estimates contested).
records.origins: An Albanian-born Ottoman officer who became governor of Egypt in 1805 and founded a dynasty. He sought a modern army independent of Ottoman Turkish troops.
records.role_summary: He invaded Sudan in 1820 to obtain gold and captives for a slave army (the jihadiyya); the Turco-Egyptian regime then raided the Nuba Mountains and the south, and private traders like al-Zubayr built slaving empires under its umbrella. Under British pressure, Khedive Ismāʿīl later hired Europeans such as Charles Gordon to suppress the trade.

roleDetail.d: The 1820–24 conquest sought Sudanese recruits for a new army; raids targeted the Nuba Mountains and the south.
In 1873 Khedive Ismāʿīl recognised al-Zubayr as governor of Bahr al-Ghazal.
Egypt signed an Anglo-Egyptian convention against the slave trade in 1877.

records.legacy: Turco-Egyptian rule and its slave raiding fed the Mahdist uprising of 1881–85. The racialised 'abid/slave' language of northern Sudan toward southerners is traced by historians to this period.

legacyDetail.d: Historians link enduring north–south hierarchies in Sudan to 19th-century slave raiding.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Trans-Saharan slave trade (survey of estimates)

connections.label: Sudanese captives via the Red Sea

lineage.name: Ibrahim Pasha
lineage.note: Commander of the armies his father built partly from enslaved Sudanese recruits.

lineage.name: Isma'il Pasha
lineage.note: Expanded Egypt in Sudan and gave the slave trader Zubayr a governorship.

lineage.name: Zubayr Pasha
lineage.note: Sudanese slave trader made governor under Isma'il.

lineage.name: Fuad II
lineage.note: Last King of Egypt as an infant (1952–53) and the dynasty's titular head.

records.today: The Muhammad Ali dynasty ruled Egypt until the monarchy was abolished in 1953; Fuad II, who reigned as an infant, is its senior living member. Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Al-Zubayr Raḥma Manṣūr (Zubayr Pasha)
records.scaleNote: From 1856 he built a network of fortified trading stations (zaribas) and a private army controlling much of Bahr al-Ghazal and parts of today's Chad and CAR; British writers called him the 'Slaver King' (numbers undocumented).
records.origins: Born near Khartoum to the Jaʿaliyyin Arab tribe. He went south in 1856 as a trader in ivory and captives.
records.role_summary: His armed zaribas raided and traded for ivory and captives, sending people north to Egypt and to Red Sea markets. Khedive Ismāʿīl recognised him as governor of Bahr al-Ghazal in 1873; he conquered Darfur in 1874 but was then detained in Cairo, while Gordon crushed his son Sulayman's revolt (1878–79).

roleDetail.d: Zaribas with private armies controlled trade routes and supplied captives.
Made governor and pasha in 1873; detained in Cairo from 1875.
Arrested in 1885 and held at Gibraltar for alleged correspondence with the Mahdi; released 1887.

records.legacy: He died at his estates near Khartoum in 1913. His former slave-soldier Rabih carried his methods west to Lake Chad.

legacyDetail.d: Rabih, once a commander in Zubayr's forces, built his own slaving state around Lake Chad.

sources.label: CUNY Academic Works — Zachary Berman, Owing and Owning: Zubayr Pasha, Slavery, and Empire in Nineteenth-Century Sudan (2017)

lineage.name: Isma'il Pasha
lineage.note: Made him a pasha and governor of Bahr el Ghazal.

lineage.name: Rabih az-Zubayr
lineage.note: His former slave-soldier, who carried his methods west.

lineage.name: Suleiman
lineage.note: Led his father's forces against Gordon's administration and was executed in 1879.

lineage.name: Charles Gordon
lineage.note: Fought his network, then in 1884 recommended him as his successor in Sudan.

records.today: After detention in Cairo and Gibraltar, Zubayr returned to Sudan in 1899 and died on his estates at Geili, north of Khartoum, in 1913. No publicly documented descendants have been traced.

records.name: Rābiḥ az-Zubayr
records.scaleNote: Conquered Bornu in 1893 and ran a slave-raiding military state until killed by the French at Kousseri in 1900 (Britannica); captive numbers are not documented.
records.origins: A Sudanese commander (enslaved as a child, per Britannica) in al-Zubayr's forces. After Sulayman's defeat in 1879 he led his men west.
records.role_summary: He raided Dar al-Kuti, Bagirmi and Wadai borderlands for captives, then took Bornu in 1893, sacking Kukawa and ruling from Dikwa. Captives were used as soldiers and traded north.

roleDetail.d: Britannica: occupied Bornu in 1893, sacking Kukawa and making Dikwa his capital.
His army was routed and he died at Kousseri in 1900.

records.legacy: His defeat opened Lake Chad to French, British and German partition. His career is a stark example of late-19th-century Sahelian slave raiding at the moment of European conquest.

legacyDetail.d: French victory at Kousseri (1900) led to the division of Bornu among colonial powers.

lineage.name: Zubayr Pasha
lineage.note: Rabih rose as a slave-soldier in Zubayr's army.

lineage.name: Suleiman
lineage.note: Zubayr's son, whose defeat sent Rabih west with his men.

lineage.name: Fadlallah bin Rabih
lineage.note: Ruled parts of Bornu after his father's death and was killed fighting France.

records.today: Rabih's state collapsed with Fadlallah's death in 1901, and the al-Kanemi shehus were restored. No publicly documented descendants have been traced.

records.name: Barbary corsair states (Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli, Salé)
records.scaleNote: Robert C. Davis estimates 1–1.25 million Europeans enslaved by North African corsairs between c. 1530 and 1780; his method (replacement rates) is debated and many historians consider it high.
records.origins: Ottoman-affiliated regencies of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli, and Moroccan Salé, licensed privateers (corsairs) in a long Mediterranean war with Christian states, which themselves enslaved Muslims on galleys.
records.role_summary: Corsairs seized ships and raided coasts as far as Ireland and Iceland, enslaving crews and villagers for labour, galleys, ransom and households. From the 1780s they captured US merchant sailors, leading to tribute treaties (1795) and the Barbary Wars.

roleDetail.d: Many captives were ransomed through religious orders or state payments; others converted and stayed.
Christian states (Malta, Livorno, Spain) also enslaved Muslims; Davis frames it as mutual 'faith slavery'.
The 1816 Anglo-Dutch bombardment freed over 1,000 captives; French conquest of Algiers in 1830 ended the system.

records.legacy: Barbary captivity shaped early US naval policy and the founding of the Navy. The topic is sometimes misused online to minimise the Atlantic trade; the scales, racial logic and hereditary status of the two systems differed greatly.

legacyDetail.d: Congress's 1794 Naval Act responded to Algerian captures of US sailors.
Historians caution against 'white slavery' narratives that equate Barbary captivity with the hereditary, racialised Atlantic system.

sources.label: Ohio State University News — Research reveals massive extent of slavery between Muslims and Christians (Robert C. Davis)
US Office of the Historian — Barbary Wars, 1801–1805 and 1815–1816

lineage.name: Oruç Reis and Hayreddin Barbarossa
lineage.note: Corsair brothers who placed Algiers under the Ottomans.

lineage.name: Murat Reis
lineage.note: Dutch convert who raided as far as Iceland and Ireland.

lineage.name: Husainid dynasty (Tunis)
lineage.note: Beys of Tunis.

lineage.name: Karamanli dynasty (Tripoli)
lineage.note: Rulers of Tripoli who fought the United States in the Barbary Wars.

records.today: The corsair regencies ended with the French conquest of Algiers (1830) and Ottoman reassertion in Tripoli (1835); Tunisia's Husainid beys ruled until 1957. No individual descendants are named here.

records.name: Murat Reis the Younger (Jan Janszoon)
records.scaleNote: Took part in the 1627 corsair raids on Iceland and led the 1631 Sack of Baltimore, Ireland, in which over 100 villagers (c. 107) were taken to Algiers (History Ireland).
records.origins: A Dutch sailor from Haarlem captured by corsairs in 1618, he converted to Islam and became a corsair captain at Algiers and Salé, later admiral of the Republic of Salé.
records.role_summary: He commanded raids that enslaved Europeans for sale in North African markets, including the Sack of Baltimore (1631). His career shows that 'Barbary' corsairing drew heavily on European renegades.

roleDetail.d: Corsairs under his command took villagers from Baltimore, County Cork, to Algiers; few returned.
European converts were prominent among corsair captains.

records.legacy: Baltimore commemorates the raid; Murat Reis is a figure of fascination in Dutch, Irish and Moroccan popular history.

legacyDetail.d: The 1631 sack is remembered locally in Baltimore, Co. Cork.

sources.label: History Ireland — From Baltimore to Barbary: the 1631 sack of Baltimore

lineage.name: Soutgen Gave
lineage.note: Dutch wife in Haarlem.

lineage.name: Lysbeth Janszoon
lineage.note: Visited her father in Morocco in 1640.

lineage.name: Second wife (Cartagena)
lineage.note: A woman of Morisco background whom he married after becoming a corsair.

lineage.name: Anthony Janszoon van Salee
lineage.note: Landholder and merchant in New Netherland, known as 'Anthony the Turk'.

records.today: Through his son Anthony Janszoon van Salee, genealogists trace many American families to Murat Reis; no living individuals are named here. Baltimore in Co. Cork commemorates the 1631 raid.

records.name: Thomas Pellow
records.scaleNote: His 1740 narrative of 23 years' captivity in Morocco is one of the best-known Barbary captivity accounts.
records.origins: A Cornish boy from Penryn, captured at sea by Salé corsairs in 1715 (some sources say 1716) aged about eleven.
records.role_summary: Enslaved by Moulay Ismāʿīl, he was forced to convert, served in the sultan's household and army, and escaped in 1738, returning to Cornwall. His narrative describes European captives' labour at Meknès.

roleDetail.d: Taken by Salé corsairs in 1715 and given to Moulay Ismāʿīl.
After 23 years he escaped and published his story in c. 1740.

records.legacy: Giles Milton's 'White Gold' (2004) popularised his story. Historians use it carefully, as captivity narratives were shaped for European readers.

legacyDetail.d: Captivity narratives are valuable but partisan sources.

sources.label: Historic UK — The Remarkable Life of Thomas Pellow
Ohio State University News — Research reveals massive extent of slavery between Muslims and Christians (Robert C. Davis)

lineage.name: Thomas Pellow and Elizabeth Lyttleton
lineage.note: His family in Penryn, Cornwall, who barely recognised him on his return in 1738.

lineage.name: John Pellow
lineage.note: Captain of the ship on which he was captured.

lineage.name: Moulay Ismail
lineage.note: Sultan whose household and army Pellow was forced to serve.

lineage.name: Wife and daughter
lineage.note: Given a wife by the sultan; both she and their daughter died while he was campaigning.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. His narrative was republished in 1890 and popularised by Giles Milton's 'White Gold' (2004).

records.name: Menelik II of Ethiopia and the Red Sea trade
records.scaleNote: Ethiopia and its southern frontier (Oromo, Sidama, Gurage) supplied much of the 19th-century Red Sea trade, estimated at c. 500,000 people for the century (Miran, cited); Menelik banned the open trade but southern expansion produced many captives.
records.origins: King of Shewa from 1865 and Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889. He defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.
records.role_summary: His southward conquests incorporated Oromo and other peoples, many of whom were enslaved and traded internally and to Red Sea and Gulf markets, despite his formal prohibitions (1876, 1889). Taxes on the trade benefited the state and nobility.

roleDetail.d: Menelik outlawed the open slave trade, yet Oromo captives were still sold in large numbers in Yemen around 1900.
Abir notes the Red Sea trade mainly supplied young women for Arabian households and harems.

records.legacy: Slavery was abolished in Ethiopia in 1942 under Haile Selassie, after the issue had been used by Italy to justify its 1935 invasion. Oromo scholars (Mekuria Bulcha) document the Oromo diaspora created by the trade.

legacyDetail.d: Ethiopia formally abolished slavery in 1942; it had joined the League of Nations in 1923 on condition of ending it.
Mussolini cited Ethiopian slavery as a pretext for invasion — another example of abolition rhetoric serving empire.

lineage.name: Sahle Selassie
lineage.note: Negus of Shewa, who named him Menelik.

lineage.name: Haile Melekot
lineage.note: Negus of Shewa.

lineage.name: Tewodros II
lineage.note: Held him prisoner at Magdala but, Menelik said, 'loved me like a son'.

lineage.name: Taytu Betul
lineage.note: Empress and co-founder of Addis Ababa.

lineage.name: Zewditu
lineage.note: Empress in her own right from 1916.

lineage.name: Lij Iyasu
lineage.note: Designated emperor 1913–1916, never crowned.

lineage.name: Zera Yacob Amha Selassie
lineage.note: Grandson of Haile Selassie; heads the exiled Solomonic house today.

records.today: Ethiopia's monarchy was abolished in 1974; the Imperial House is headed by Zera Yacob Amha Selassie, grandson of Haile Selassie (Menelik's successor), recognised by the Crown Council since 1997. Menelik is honoured for the 1896 victory at Adwa, while Oromo and other southern historians stress the conquest and enslavement that funded his state. Present-day descendants and members of the royal house carry no guilt for their ancestors' slave trading.

records.name: Sir John Kirk
records.scaleNote: As British consul (1866–87) he negotiated the 1873 treaty that closed the Zanzibar slave market (Britannica; The National Archives).
records.origins: A Scottish doctor and botanist who accompanied David Livingstone's Zambezi expedition (1858–63).
records.role_summary: As agent and consul-general in Zanzibar he pressed Sultan Barghash to sign the 1873 treaty, monitored smuggling, and documented the trade in letters to the Anti-Slavery Society. He also advanced British imperial interests, helping prepare the protectorate.

roleDetail.d: Concluded the 1873 anti-slave-trade treaty with Barghash.
His anti-slavery diplomacy was also a lever for British influence over Zanzibar.

records.legacy: His papers are held by the National Library of Scotland. He is remembered both as an abolitionist and as an architect of British influence in East Africa.

legacyDetail.d: The National Library of Scotland holds his correspondence on the slave trade.

sources.label: The National Archives (UK) — The last slave market: Dr John Kirk and the struggle to end the African slave trade
National Library of Scotland — Out of Africa: The Kirk Papers

lineage.name: David Livingstone
lineage.note: Kirk served as doctor and botanist on the Zambezi expedition.

lineage.name: Bartle Frere
lineage.note: His mission prepared the treaty Kirk persuaded Barghash to sign.

lineage.name: Barghash bin Said
lineage.note: Sultan with whom Kirk negotiated the closure of the slave market.

records.today: Kirk's papers and photographs are held by the National Library of Scotland. No living descendants are named here.

records.name: David Livingstone
records.scaleNote: His report of the Nyangwe massacre (15 July 1871), in which Arab-Swahili traders' men killed hundreds at a market, helped spur the 1873 closure of the Zanzibar market.
records.base: Ujiji (Lake Tanganyika) on his last journey
records.origins: A Scottish missionary-doctor of the London Missionary Society who explored southern and central Africa from 1841.
records.role_summary: He publicised the East African slave trade, calling it an 'open sore', and urged 'Christianity, commerce and civilisation' as a remedy. His account of Nyangwe, carried home by Stanley, caused outrage in Britain in 1872.

roleDetail.d: His diary records 300–500 killed, mostly women at market; recent spectral imaging of the diary (Livingstone Online) shows his own party may have been implicated.
He travelled with and was supplied by Arab-Swahili traders, including Tippu Tip.

records.legacy: His death in 1873 and burial in Westminster Abbey made him an icon of Victorian anti-slavery, later used to justify colonial expansion in Africa.

legacyDetail.d: A critical digital edition of his 1871 field diary revises his published account.
His legacy was mobilised for British colonialism in Central Africa.

sources.label: Britannica — David Livingstone: The Zambezi expedition
Smithsonian Libraries — David Livingstone and the Other Slave Trade, Part III

lineage.name: Neil and Agnes Livingstone
lineage.note: Poor Blantyre family; his father was a Sunday-school teacher and tea seller.

lineage.name: Robert Moffat
lineage.note: Missionary at Kuruman who drew Livingstone to Africa.

lineage.name: Mary Moffat Livingstone
lineage.note: Moffat's daughter; died on the Zambezi expedition.

lineage.name: John Kirk
lineage.note: Zambezi expedition doctor, later consul in Zanzibar.

lineage.name: Tippu Tip
lineage.note: Livingstone travelled with Arab-Swahili caravans in the interior.

lineage.name: Henry Morton Stanley
lineage.note: Found him at Ujiji in 1871.

lineage.name: Susi, Chuma and Jacob Wainwright
lineage.note: African companions who carried his body to the coast.

records.today: Livingstone's birthplace at Blantyre, Scotland, is a museum, and the Zambian town of Livingstone keeps his name. His legacy is contested: an icon of Victorian anti-slavery, he was also used to justify colonial rule. No living descendants are named here.

records.name: Zanzibar slave market (Mkunazini) and Christ Church Cathedral
records.description: The main open slave market of 19th-century East Africa, in Stone Town, where captives from the mainland were sold for Zanzibar and Pemba clove plantations and for export to Arabia and the Gulf. It was closed under the 1873 Frere treaty; the Universities' Mission to Central Africa bought the site and laid the foundation of Christ Church Cathedral on Christmas Day 1873, with the altar reputedly over the whipping post. A memorial of chained figures and holding cells now forms a heritage site there.

connections.label: part of site given by Jairam Senji

records.name: Kilwa Kisiwani and Kilwa Kivinje
records.description: Medieval Swahili city-state, sacked by the Portuguese in 1505, which revived in the 18th century chiefly through the slave trade. From the 1770s Kilwa supplied French Mascarene planters; in the 19th century Kilwa Kivinje on the mainland was the leading export point for captives bound for Zanzibar. Kilwa Kisiwani's ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

records.name: Island of Mozambique (Ilha de Moçambique)
records.description: Portuguese capital of Mozambique from the 16th century, with the Fortress of São Sebastião; UNESCO notes it became a slave-trading port from the second half of the 18th century. Captives from the Makua and Yao interior were shipped to Brazil, the French Mascarenes, Cuba and elsewhere. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a site in the Routes of Enslaved Peoples programme.

records.name: Mozambique–Brazil slave route (Southeast Africa to the Atlantic)
records.description: The main interplay between Indian Ocean and Atlantic slaving: SlaveVoyages estimates roughly half a million captives embarked from Southeast Africa and the Indian Ocean islands for the Americas, overwhelmingly after 1800 and mostly landed at Rio de Janeiro. The voyage around the Cape was long and mortality high (some recorded voyages exceeded 30%). The trade peaked c. 1811–1830 and continued illegally until Brazil's 1850 law.

records.name: French Mascarenes: Île de France (Mauritius) and Île Bourbon (Réunion)
records.description: French Indian Ocean plantation colonies whose enslaved population grew from c. 7,200 (1735) to c. 133,000 (1807); Allen estimates 336,000–388,000 enslaved people were brought to the islands 1670–1848, mainly from Madagascar and East Africa. Mauritius passed to Britain in 1810 (emancipation 1835); in Réunion abolition was proclaimed on 20 December 1848, after which planters recruited 'engagés' from India, Madagascar, the Comoros and Mozambique under contracts critics likened to a disguised slave trade. Le Morne, Mauritius (UNESCO, 2008) commemorates maroon resistance.

connections.label: Code Noir of 1723 for the islands

records.name: Trans-Saharan slave caravan routes (Bornu–Fezzan–Tripoli, Darb al-Arbaʿin, Timbuktu–Morocco)
records.description: Desert roads that carried captives from the Sahel to North Africa, Egypt and the Ottoman world from the 7th to the early 20th century. Ralph Austen's widely cited 'tentative census' reconstructions (1979, revised 1992) give roughly 7 million people for c. 650–1900; Olivier Pétré-Grenouilleau, building on Austen, cites c. 9 million. Early figures are inference from a thin record and all such totals are contested. Unlike the Atlantic trade, most captives were women and children destined for domestic service and concubinage; some boys were castrated before crossing, with high mortality.

records.name: Red Sea and Gulf of Aden slave route (Massawa, Suakin, Tajura to Jeddah and Mocha)
records.description: Sea routes carrying Ethiopian, Oromo and Sudanese captives to Arabia, the Hijaz and the Ottoman world; scholars estimate around 500,000 people in the 19th century alone. The trade supplied mainly young women and boys for households, and suppression took roughly a century, continuing into the 1930s. Austen's separate estimates for the Red Sea and East African (Indian Ocean) exports, c. 800–1900, together come to roughly 4 million or more; syntheses building on his work go as high as c. 8 million (Pétré-Grenouilleau). These figures are contested.

records.name: Central caravan route (Ujiji–Tabora–Bagamoyo)
records.description: The main 19th-century caravan road from Lake Tanganyika through Unyamwezi (Tabora) to the coast at Bagamoyo, opposite Zanzibar, used for ivory and captives; enslaved people often carried the ivory. Nyamwezi porters, Arab-Swahili traders and Indian financiers all shaped it. It is on Tanzania's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list as 'The Central Slave and Ivory Trade Route'.

records.name: Moresby Treaty (1822)
records.description: Agreement between Captain Fairfax Moresby (for the Governor of Mauritius) and Sayyid Saʿīd forbidding the sale of enslaved people from Omani dominions to Christians and setting a line beyond which Omani slave ships could be seized. It aimed above all to cut supply to the French Mascarenes and to British India, not to end the Arab trade.

records.name: Hamerton Treaty (1845)
records.description: Negotiated by British consul Atkins Hamerton, it bound Sayyid Saʿīd to prohibit the export of enslaved people from his African dominions to Arabia and beyond, effective 1847, while the coastal trade between Kilwa and Lamu and Zanzibar stayed legal. Enforcement by the Royal Navy was patchy.

records.name: Frere Treaty (Anglo-Zanzibari treaty of 5 June 1873)
records.description: Treaty negotiated by Sir Bartle Frere's mission and consul John Kirk, signed by Sultan Barghash under threat of a British naval blockade. It banned the seaborne transport of enslaved people from the mainland and closed public slave markets in Zanzibar's dominions, though slavery itself remained legal until 1897.

records.name: Malê Revolt, Salvador da Bahia (1835)
records.description: Uprising of enslaved and freed African Muslims (Malês, from Yoruba 'imale') in Salvador on 24–25 January 1835, during Ramadan; João José Reis calls it the most effective urban slave revolt in the Americas. Many participants were Yoruba (Nagô) and Hausa people enslaved in the wars of Oyo's collapse and the Sokoto jihad. After defeat, several hundred Africans were deported to West Africa, many joining Afro-Brazilian communities at Lagos and Ouidah.

connections.label: deportees returned to the Bight of Benin

records.name: Brussels Conference Act (1890)
records.description: International convention of European powers, the US, the Ottoman Empire, Persia and Zanzibar against the African slave trade by land and sea, including the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. It also justified colonial occupation of the African interior as anti-slavery action, notably by Leopold II's Congo Free State.

events.title: Sack of Baltimore
events.text: Corsairs under Murat Reis seized over 100 villagers from Baltimore, Co. Cork, and took them to Algiers.

source.label: History Ireland — From Baltimore to Barbary: the 1631 sack of Baltimore

events.title: Moulay Ismāʿīl founds the ʿAbīd al-Bukhārī
events.text: Morocco's sultan began building a Black slave army, eventually perhaps c. 150,000 strong per Britannica (figure contested).

events.title: US treaty with Algiers frees captive sailors
events.text: The US agreed to pay tribute to Algiers in return for the release of American sailors held there.

source.label: US Office of the Historian — Barbary Wars, 1801–1805 and 1815–1816

events.title: Usman dan Fodio's jihad begins
events.text: The Fulani-led jihad overthrew the Hausa kings and created the Sokoto Caliphate, whose wars produced captives for internal slavery, the Sahara and the Atlantic.

events.title: Bombardment of Algiers
events.text: An Anglo-Dutch fleet under Lord Exmouth bombarded Algiers; the Dey freed 1,083 Christian captives.

events.title: Egypt invades Sudan
events.text: Muḥammad ʿAlī's forces invaded Sudan seeking gold and enslaved recruits, opening decades of slave raiding.

events.title: Moresby Treaty
events.text: Sayyid Saʿīd agreed to stop sales of enslaved people to Christians, aimed at the French Mascarene trade.

events.title: Malê Revolt in Bahia
events.text: African Muslims, many captured in the Sokoto jihad and Oyo wars, rose in Salvador; hundreds were later deported to Africa.

source.label: BlackPast — The Malê Rebellion in Brazil (1835)

events.title: Hamerton Treaty
events.text: Sayyid Saʿīd agreed to ban slave exports from his African dominions to Arabia, leaving the coastal trade legal.

events.title: Abolition in Réunion; engagés follow
events.text: Abolition was proclaimed in Réunion on 20 December 1848; planters turned to indentured 'engagés' from India, Madagascar and East Africa.

source.label: Portail de l'esclavage de La Réunion

events.title: Brazil's Eusébio de Queirós law
events.text: Brazil's effective ban on imports ended the Mozambique–Brazil Atlantic route, pushing Southeast African captives toward Indian Ocean markets instead.

events.title: Nyangwe massacre
events.text: Livingstone witnessed traders' gunmen kill hundreds at Nyangwe market; his report caused outrage in Britain.

events.title: Zanzibar slave market closed
events.text: Under threat of blockade, Sultan Barghash signed the Frere treaty on 5 June; the UMCA began Christ Church on the market site that Christmas.

source.label: The National Archives (UK) — The last slave market: Dr John Kirk and the struggle to end the African slave trade

events.title: Brussels Anti-Slavery Act
events.text: European powers, the Ottoman Empire, Persia and Zanzibar agreed measures against the land and sea slave trade, also legitimising colonial conquest.
